The Prophet was the most generous of people, and most of all in Ramadan when Gabriel met him every night to teach him the Quran.
The Prophet repeated what he said three times so it would be understood, and asked permission to enter by knocking three times with a greeting.
The Prophet liked to begin with the right side in putting on shoes, combing his hair, washing himself and everything else.
Goods from Bahrain were spread in the mosque; after prayer the Prophet gave them out to everyone until none remained, refusing to help Al-Abbas lift his overloaded garment.
The Prophet liked to start everything from the right where possible, as in washing, combing and wearing shoes.
The Prophet was seen lying on his back in the mosque with one leg over the other, as Umar and Uthman also did.
The Prophet clasped his hands by interlacing his fingers.
The Prophet opened addresses with the Tashahhud, praise and 'Amma ba'du', as when explaining why he gave to some and not others, and why he stopped leading the night prayer.
The Prophet ate a tailor's meal, picking out the gourd, and wore a sheet a woman wove him, then gave it to a man wanting it for his shroud.
Abdullah bin Amr said the Torah describes the Prophet as witness, bearer of glad tidings and warner, Al-Mutawakkil, neither harsh nor loud in markets, forgiving evildoers, and opening blind eyes.
Abu Talha brought the boy Anas to serve the Prophet at home and on journeys, and the Prophet never asked him why he did or left anything.
The Prophet, best, bravest and most generous, rides out ahead when Medina takes fright, and, mobbed by bedouins after Hunain, says they will find him no miser, liar or coward.
The Prophet was the most generous and bravest; when Medina took fright at night he rode Abu Talha's unsaddled horse with his sword, telling people not to be scared.
The Prophet's ring, engraved Muhammad Apostle Allah, seals Abu Bakr's letter; Anas shows his worn shoes, Aisha the patched garment he died in, and his cup is mended with silver.
Abu Bakr pays Jabir what the Prophet promised him from Bahrain's revenue; the Prophet distributes Bahrain's money in the mosque till none remains, refusing to help al-Abbas lift his share.
Al-Hasan resembled the Prophet; companions describe him as of medium height, rosy, handsome and moon-faced, with few white hairs, his hand colder than ice and more fragrant than musk.
The Prophet was most generous in Ramadan, beamed when happy, chose the easier course, took revenge only for Allah, was shy, and never spoke obscenely or faulted food.
The Prophet's armpits showed in prostration and rain prayer, his words could be counted, he prayed no more than eleven rak'at, and his eyes slept but not his heart.
The Prophet only smiled, never laughing loudly, and showed concern at clouds and wind, fearing punishment, as some people were punished by a wind they took for rain.
Aisha said the Prophet worked for his family at home and went out when he heard the adhan.
People sought the Prophet's leftover ablution water at his red leather tent; he prayed at night within a mat screen, urging steady deeds, and kept a gold-buttoned cloak for Makhrama.
Handsome in a red cloak, the Prophet was neither tall nor short, his hair neither curly nor straight; sent at forty, he died at sixty with barely ten white hairs.
The Prophet's wavy hair hung to his shoulders or just above, and he had big hands and feet, soft palms and a good-looking face, unlike anyone else.
Abbad's uncle saw the Prophet lying down in the mosque with one leg placed over the other.
Sensing young men staying twenty nights missed their families, the kind-hearted Prophet sent them home to teach them, pray as he prayed, give the Adhan and let the eldest lead.
The Prophet, brave and generous, never spoke obscenely or refused requests, urged Aisha to gentleness and was polite to a man he called evil; the best have the best character.
Anas served the Prophet ten years without ever hearing a word of impatience or blame, and at home the Prophet served his family until prayer time.
The Prophet called a man evil before admitting him, then spoke to him politely, saying the worst people are those others avoid for fear of their foul tongue or wrongdoing.
Any slave girl of Medina could take the Prophet by the hand and lead him wherever she wished, Anas said.
The Prophet ate with an Ansari household, prayed in their house on a mat sprinkled with water, and invoked Allah's blessing on his hosts.
The Prophet smiled rather than laughing aloud: at Rifa'a's divorced wife, women hiding from Umar, a poor man's Ramadan offence, a rough bedouin, Jarir, and rain prayers.
The Prophet was shyer than a virgin in her room, and when he disliked something it showed on his face.
The Prophet joked with young Abu Umair about his bird, called back Aisha's playmates at dolls, spoke gently to a man he called evil, and saved Makhrama a cloak.
The Prophet, best in character, would ask Anas's little brother about his pet bird, and at prayer time in their house led them in prayer on a swept, sprinkled carpet.
Ibn Umar saw the Prophet sitting in the courtyard of the Ka'bah in the ihtiba posture, his hand round his legs.
The Prophet once hurried home after the Asr prayer, and he prayed in the middle of his bed while Aisha lay before him and slipped quietly away.
Um Sulaim spread a leather sheet for the Prophet's midday nap and mixed his sweat and hair into perfume, some of which Anas had added to his embalming perfume.
The Prophet was seen lying on his back in the mosque with one leg over the other.
The Prophet chose the easier of two options unless it was sinful, and never took revenge for himself, only for Allah's sake when His limits were transgressed.
Anas, brought as a boy to serve the Prophet at home and on journeys, said the Prophet never asked him why he had or had not done anything.
